105.t: How the pianoless cello quintet came together
105.s: John Graas dies, Fred Katz joins, and the group rehearsed in his living room like the Mulligan Quartet.
105.q: Originally the group was going to be French horn, John Graas, he was the number one French horn player on the West Coast at that time when I formed the group. The group was intact with Buddy and Jim Hall, and Carson. And Buddy and I came up musically together. Cars and I were with Gerry together,…

105.s: Mulligan had already lined up Chet Baker and Bob Whitlock; they rehearsed in Hamilton's living room and, he says, simply happened to be the right four at the right time.
105.ch: Package tours and the original quintet
105.q: Well, as I found out later, Gerry had been looking -- you know, decided to form a group and by the time he told me about it he had already decided -- he had talked with Chet Baker already and he already had Bob Whitlock, and so it was just a question of me and me being available. You know, I said…

105.s: Unable to hire a piano trio he built the group with Jim Hall, Carson Smith, Buddy Collette and a cellist, Fred Katz, after his French horn player died.
105.ch: Package tours and the original quintet
105.q: In all honesty that happened just by sheer accident. How I come about with the original quintet is that at first I wanted to get Gerry Wiggins, get a piano trio, but all the piano players that I liked, man, they had their own thing going so I decided to try something else. So I don’t know how I got…

144.t: Early sextets: Al Aarons, Joe Henderson, Hank Mobley and Dorham
144.s: Fuller recalls trying a small group with Joe Henderson and Al Aarons in Detroit, and then forming the sextet with Kenny Dorham and Hank Mobley.
144.q: The first call to arms with the Jazztet… Well, I actually tried in school first with Joe Henderson and Albert Aarons, a trumpet player in Ohio who actually ended up one of the most pronounced players in the jazz scene in the West Coast. I couldn't get Quincy Jones to hire him but Albert was the…

144.t: Kenny Dorham's writing, three-horn bands and the Five Spot gig that led to the Jazztet
144.s: Fuller describes loving three-horn writing, working with Thad Jones, replacing Monk at the Five Spot with Golson and how the Jazztet came about.
144.q: a very good player. His lines were impeccable, you know? His playing lines… He wrote some beautiful sextet arrangements, you know? If you go back and listen to "Lotus Flower” those pretty things that Kenny Dorham wrote, have you ever heard it? He did it with JJ and Cecil. It goes like this (sings…

144.t: Forming the Jazztet: McCoy Tyner, Steve Allen's backing and Art Farmer joining
144.s: Fuller tells how Art Farmer joined, Steve Allen financed rehearsals, McCoy Tyner moved to New York and the group meant to be a cooperative.
144.q: Art came in as the other group. They always hire two groups at The Five Spot. First, it was Randy Weston and his quartet. So, Art came in with Jerry Mulligan. The first (inaudible), Benny said, "Curtis, going to try and put a group together. You write good for sextet. Why don't we get this group? I…

739.t: Chico Hamilton, Mulligan and the pianoless quartet
739.s: Poston discusses the tension between Hamilton and Mulligan and how the pianoless quartet came about.
739.q: Yeah I mean there’s some of that. Chico and Gerry didn’t get along too well after Chico left. And you would think that years later they would have let that go. Well Gerry didn’t let things go very well. But Chico left the group to go with Lena Horne when the group had really hit you know. And Gerry…

739.t: Chico Hamilton's cello group as an accident
739.s: Poston confirms the story that Fred Katz played piano parts on cello at the Strollers Club.
739.q: Yeah. I mean that was, you know, according to everybody it was an accident. And that’s according to all of them: Chico, Buddy, Jim Hall, Fred Katz. I mean they all agreed that it all happened with Fred playing — you know Fred was a very accomplished cellist and I mean he looked like a cellist — I…

278.s: The Meters were already a group, Art Neville's band at the Ivanhoe; compared to Booker T and the MGs.
278.ch: Sansu, Irma, Lee Dorsey and the Meters
278.q: No, they were together, very much so. Art Neville and the Neville Sound, playing at the Ivanhoe. A great little band. And that's how they came.

204.t: Taking up baritone, the Cafe Bohemia and meeting Mulligan and Carney
204.s: A borrowed baritone led to buying one; at Cafe Bohemia with the Ithaca college group opposite Buddy Rich, Mulligan introduced him to Harry Carney.
204.q: Actually in 1956 maybe? My alto was — this is on the back of one of my albums, I can’t remember which one. But my alto needed some repair and as usual I’d take it to the music store. And they always let me take an alto. They had no altos but they had a baritone. So I said “I don’t want to play…

737.t: The late-arriving Sonny at the festival, the Rollins group and leaving for Joe Williams
737.s: Rollins showed up after a long Dixieland set and the trio tore the place up; Cranshaw later joined his group with Perkins and Jim Hall, then left when it became free-form and went with Joe Williams.
737.q: it was really a very funny situation ‘cause it was in the afternoon on a Sunday afternoon. Sonny Rollins told us to be there I think the concert maybe started at one o’clock or two, I think about two. Sonny said well be there, ready to play at one. I get there, and we don’t see no Sonny. Two…

842.t: First night at Hamilton and meeting Derry Hall
842.s: He hears pianist Derry Hall his first night, plays with him, then meets Emerson and the Catatonic Five forms.
842.q: So that all sort of fell together. And I can remember that first night I was at Hamilton I heard somebody over at what we used to call Silliman Hall playing the piano, and it was Derry Hall.

133.t: Joining Benny Golson and Art Farmer's Jazztet for ten dollars more
133.s: A ten dollar raise took him and Albert Heath into the Jazztet; Golson wrote everything, which forced Walton back to reading, and Art Blakey then called after remembering him from before the Army.
133.q: Uh, a ten dollar raise. You know, back in those days that ten dollars was that important. [chuckles] So … Me and Albert Heath uh both uh moved over to the Jazztet, replacing uh McCoy Tyner and uh, uh, oh, let me see, who was it? Might have been on drums. Oh, Lex Humphries is the guy that had been…

110.t: The Marines Memorial concert and how the trio was born
110.s: Pressed to put his name on the octet concert, he then gets NBC's Jimmy Lyons and Maria Corbin interested, leading to a trio radio show.
110.q: Technically, the octet should have been called something like the workshop ensemble. It wasn’t under my name, because we were all equals as far as talent goes. Again, Iola will know the man’s name who wanted to produce us like the octet. We ran into him recently someplace. I should never forget…

527.t: Joining Horace Silver's group and recording his own sessions
527.s: Horace Silver's band after the Messengers, Hank Mobley and Clifford Jordan, and Farmer's early Prestige albums.
527.q: Yeah, it must have been around ’55, somewhere around then. Then, I started getting gigs with Horace Silver. Horace had been with Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers, which was a co-op group supposedly, with Hank Mobley and Kenny Durham. The bass player…

491.t: Forming the Jazztet with Art Farmer
491.s: After leaving Blakey, Golson and Art Farmer independently planned a sextet; Curtis Fuller suggested the name Jazztet, first used at the Roundtable.
491.q: Yeah. After I came back to New York, like I told him, I wanted to establish myself as a writer, writing for this and that, whatever the situation was. During that time, I can remember I did things for Dinah Washington, and I did lots of commercials for all kinds of products, and other things I’ve…

328.s: Between Dizzy and the octet he joined Blakey with McCoy Tyner, Joe Henderson, Bill Hardman and Junie Booth.
328.q: Yeah. I joined the band. When I joined the band, McCoy Tyner was there. Joe Henderson, Bill Hardman, Junie Booth, and Art. They played music that would move you right off the stage if you didn’t hold on. It was so strong that it was frightening. You can imagine, with McCoy and Art in the same band.…

225.t: The quintet with Nat Adderley and the Columbia contract
225.s: Johnson formed a trumpet and trombone quintet with neighbor Nat Adderley, leading to an exclusive Columbia contract.
225.q: I had heard about Nat, and I was so impressed with Nat. Then Nat and I became neighbors. In a cycle when I lived in Teaneck, New Jersey, Nat and his wife Ann also lived in Teaneck, New Jersey. We really became fast friends then and there. When I thought about formulating a different texture…

460.s: Laws recalls playing alto flute and flute on Herbie Hancock's The Prisoner at Van Gelder's and admires Herbie's writing.
460.ch: The Met orchestra and joining CTI
460.q: Yes I do. I kind of remember that. I do remember that he had me playing alto flute on it, for sure. Alto flute, C flute, and . . .

508.t: Seeing Wynton in the Blakey band; hearing Nefertiti; disliking post-bop
508.s: The Blakey group's lineup and group-first ethos, Smitty Smith playing him Nefertiti, and his dislike of regimented post-bop.
508.ch: Southern, Berklee and becoming a jazz player
508.q: It’s a very important distinction. Very important. With Wynton on trumpet, Bobby Watson on alto, Billy Pierce tenor, Charles Fambrough on bass, James Williams on piano and Bu, Art Blakey on drums. And it was just something about the concept of it – where you have this group and every person in the…
